documents.abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

High-quality data is essential for improving instruction tuning in threat intelligence analysis. However, existing methods for generating cybersecurity instruction data lack reliable quality assessment mechanisms, and gradient influence-based data selection methods primarily focus on single-sample matching, failing to cover diverse and complex security capabilities. To address these issues, we propose CTI-TDS, a Targeted Data Selection method for instruction tuning in Cyber Threat Intelligence analysis. Specifically, we first filter high-quality CTI instructions by integrating instruction style consistency and security knowledge verification. Furthermore, we formulate gradient influence as a distribution alignment problem, learning a gradient subspace of target tasks and applying entropic regularized optimal transport to optimize distribution matching between training samples and target tasks, enabling diversity-aware data selection. We conduct extensive experiments on CTIBench across multiple large language models. Experimental results demonstrate that when fine-tuning with only a small set of high-value instruction data, CTI-TDS outperforms existing data selection methods and achieves competitive performance on threat intelligence analysis tasks.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The article presents the results of an action-research project that aimed to model and validated the contributions of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) AI as a learning resource in the core curricular lines of the social work formation process. The research responds to the need to model the inclusion GenAI as a learning resource in the university training of disciplines focused on human connection such as social work . Worked with a section of 18 students from the fourth semester of the course, selected by non-probabilistic sampling for convenience A cycle of four work sessions with GenAI was carried out, which was compatible with the training activities of the theoretical-methodological curricular lines of Social Sciences and theoretical-practical social work carried out in the selected subject. The expected results were oriented towards obtaining definitions with GenAI support, collation reflections, GenAI support in writing professional documents and methodological mapping. The validation of GenAI as a learning resource is concluded, with support from teachers and students. In addition, it is confirmed that social intervention occupies a central place in vocational training, which displaces AIGen from an assessment of centrality initially assigned by the digital native student generations, towards a limited and complementary contribution position that adds to the repertoire of available learning resources.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AIM: The transition from medical school to surgical residency is marked by a persistent gap between theoretical instruction and clinical readiness. In Italy, variability in training programs across centers creates persistent gaps in residents’ medical education. Scientific societies are asked to identify current training gaps and define the core competencies required for effective surgical training. We propose an undergraduate curriculum to support last-year medical students in Italy.METHODS: A scoping review of the literature focusing on structured surgical curricula for undergraduate medical students was conducted. A suggested “curriculum” was introduced at the 2025 Congress of the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons (SPIGC) in Bari, Italy.RESULTS: The SPIGC curriculum includes seven domains: (1) soft skills: communication, informed consent, and interdisciplinary collaboration; (2) clinical and diagnostic skills: outpatient clinic management and perioperative care; (3) hygiene, prevention, healthcare systems; (4) technical skills; (5) emergency and trauma surgery; (6) perioperative management, integrating Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols, nutritional assessment, and infections; (7) evidence-based medicine and recommendations. The SPIGC curriculum highlights the importance of simulation labs, hands-on workshops, and online learning, while providing clear pathways for fellowships or masters. It also introduces artificial intelligence (AI) systems as a modern learning tool, while highlighting the importance of their safe and responsible use.CONCLUSIONS: The SPIGC curriculum may provide a structured plan to improve surgical education for medical students in Italy and to align it with international standards. Its acceptability and impact on training quality and patient outcomes remain to be evaluated through future consensus and prospective studies.
keywords: transition from medical school to residency

documents.abstract: The early detection of Parkinson's disease (PD) is critical for timely and effective clinical intervention and disease management. High dimensional gene expression data redundancy features, class imbalance and limited interpretability are challenges discussed for transcriptomic-based diagnostic approaches. To overcome these drawbacks, TransVaTabNet, new approach that combines transcriptomic analysis, deep learning and explainable artificial intelligence detect PD and discover biomarkers. The RNA-seq data is first pre-processed by low expression gene filtering, Trimmed Mean of M-values normalization, and voom transformation. The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are determined through the framework of Limma-voom, and are then subjected to stage-specific gene analysis and functional enrichment to map the disease-related biological pathways. The high dimensional gene expression profiles are learned to a compact latent representation using a Variational AutoEncoder, and SMOTE is used to deal with class imbalance. The derived features are then classified with a TabNet model that adopts a sequential attention mechanism to attend to informative transcriptomic patterns. In addition, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used for model interpretability and biomarker identification. Experimental results on the GSE216281 RNA-seq dataset are shown to validate the proposed framework with 90.95% Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), outperforming the classical machine learning models. The results show that TransVaTabNet can provide an accurate, interpretable and biologically meaningful framework for stage-specific detection PD and biomarker discovery, which can support precision diagnosis and further clinical decisions.

Society is evolving and so too (finally) are the plans of modern financial institutions. This is because corporate sustainability has moved away from business as usual and is instead utilized to grow competitive advantage by increasing choice for employees and power-with stakeholders to pursue non-traditional routes. This makes robust financial management in the financial industry imperative to uphold sustainable practices and advance. Successful financial management now combines its primary duties with artificial intelligence (AI) to monitor, evaluate, and execute projects within the time constraints set. A few important credit decisions made during the growth or expansion of credit options were significantly improved using an array of AI techniques in this case. This method is so well used by finance managers that they have the ability to watch over all of their offices or a single transaction within any part of them.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence models and systems capable of acting semi-autonomously has exacerbated issues relating to the processing of personal data, profiling and automated decision-making. The average user is unaware of the true extent to which their personal information is processed, what data is collected, how long it is retained, for what purpose it is used, or which third parties may access it. This situation leads to a gradual loss of effective control over personal information and calls into question the adequacy of consent as the primary mechanism legitimising data processing. This phenomenon is particularly significant on everyday digital platforms such as Spotify, where artificial intelligence plays an essential role in generating music recommendations, personalising content and developing behavioural profiles through the continuous analysis of activity carried out within the platform.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Voice-based assistants (VBAs) such as Alexa and Siri are widely used in everyday life and increasingly act as information intermediaries. Their human-like voices and behaviors can elicit social responses, while new assistants based on large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT voice mode, further blur the boundaries between machine and human communicators. Despite risks associated with misinformation and limited data transparency, adoption remains high. Trust may be relevant to users’ relationships with conversational AI, but there is little consensus on how it should be conceptualized. Technical, interpersonal, and media trust frameworks may all be applicable. This multi-method qualitative study examined users’ subjective concepts of trust through 22 in-home interviews complemented by observational tasks involving participants’ own VBAs and ChatGPT voice mode. Participants drew on interpersonal concepts when defining trust but commonly restricted trust in VBAs to particular tasks and functions. Technical and media-related trustworthiness criteria were especially prominent, whereas social responses and anthropomorphic qualities did not necessarily translate into interpersonal trust. Experience, calibrated expectations, selective use, habitual engagement, and trust were described as closely interrelated. Although ChatGPT was often evaluated positively, particularly as an information intermediary, its perceived capabilities were not uniformly accompanied by greater trust compared with participants’ familiar VBAs. Based on these findings, we propose a preliminary conceptual framework of task-specific hybrid trust in VBAs.

Medical image analysis has been revolutionized by the advent of artificial intelligence, which has made automated disease detection, segmentation and diagnosis possible across a range of imaging modalities, thus supporting clinical decisions. However, the increasing complexity of deep learning models has raised concerns regarding their reliability, interpretability, fairness, privacy, and regulatory compliance, highlighting the need for trustworthy AI in healthcare. The review focuses on recent breakthroughs in deep learning models for medical image analysis, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), segmentation networks based on U-net, Vision Transformers, and foundation models, and explores their use in clinical decision support. It also examines the fundamental principles of trustworthy AI, including explainability, robustness, fairness, privacy preservation, reliability, transparency and regulatory governance. The review summarizes the current state of the art for the strengths and limitations of current AI models and highlights some of the challenges that hamper the use of these models in the clinical workflow, such as limited data availability, domain shifts, algorithmic bias, computational complexity, and integration into the clinical workflow. New concepts like multimodal foundation models, federated learning and privacy-preserving AI are also explored as potential advancements in the safe, scalable and clinically relevant use of AI in medical imaging. The review highlights the significant progress medical image analysis has made using deep learning techniques but emphasizes that the effective translation of these technologies into clinical practice requires both technical advancement and adherence to trustworthy AI principles and effective governance models. To ensure these AI systems are effective for patient care and to aid in evidence-based medical decision making, development needs continued cooperation between researchers, clinicians, healthcare institutions and regulatory bodies, with the aim of creating reliable, transparent and clinically acceptable AI systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer deployed as bare models. They run inside an execution harness, the control layer that assembles context, exposes tools, manages memory and state, schedules retries, and verifies intermediate results. Because the harness determines what the model sees and what its outputs are allowed to do, observed agent behavior is jointly produced by the model and the harness, yet prevailing benchmarks attribute it to the model alone. We study the problem of harness evaluation: holding the model, task distribution, environment, budget, and evaluator fixed, how can the contribution of the harness be isolated, and what does it mean for a harness to be trustworthy? We formalize the harness as a trajectory-generating policy and define the harness effect as a paired, metric-indexed contrast. We then develop measurement principles along seven dimensions—outcome correctness, quality, efficiency, reliability and reproducibility, robustness, safety, and fairness—each targeting the specific mechanisms through which a harness influences agent behavior, and grounded in established results from statistical evaluation, efficient inference, certified robustness, and fair learning. A set of elementary propositions clarifies when paired designs reduce variance, how approximate verification bounds correctness loss, why marginal subgroup gaps can mislead, and how differential evaluator bias contaminates harness comparisons. We conclude with a reference protocol and argue that harness quality should be reported as a Pareto profile rather than a single leaderboard score.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.

Counts of which brands a large language model names are useful only if they hold long enough to act on. We test this with a pre-registered replication. The same 162 requests (54 questions in English, Estonian and Finnish about three software categories, four of twelve candidate brands per question, three repeats) were sent to gemini-3.1-pro-preview in three waves within about ten hours on 22 and 23 September 2026, and again on 13 October 2026, 20.3 days after the third wave, with identical request bodies. The plan and its decision rule were frozen, hashed and registered on OSF before the first call. The outcome is a lexical mention label per answer and brand, 648 per wave. The primary forecast, each brand-and-question cell's mention rate over the nine earlier answers, scored Brier 0.0281 and log loss 0.126, against Brier 0.0259 for the six-answer forecast of the 8-hour wave and a registered ceiling of 0.0559. It beat brand history (0.104), the overall rate (0.234) and a constant 0.5 (0.250) on both scores and in all nine question families (exact sign-flip p = 0.0039), so durability holds under the registered rule. A forecast frozen from the first wave alone scored 0.0599, 0.0587 and 0.0604 at horizons of 1.5 hours, 9.6 hours and 20.7 days. Of the 202 cells unanimous in the 8-hour wave, 194 were unchanged at D1 and none reversed. The latest wave alone was nearly as accurate as the pooled history (Brier 0.0292; pooled lower in 5 of 9 families, p = 0.28). Every answer reported the requested model version, and none issued a search query although search was enabled. A blind human check of 96 labels agreed with the rule on 94; both disagreements were adjudicated as rater omissions, so after adjudication the rule matched on 96 of 96. The test covers one model, one interval and twelve known brands, and estimates no decay rate.

Abstract: Both ARPA-H and the FDA recently launched programs to help accelerate clinical trials. ARPA-H announced the SURPASS program, which is intended to create faster clinical trials that are more cost-effective and have fewer participants than current studies. It is seeking ideas from cross-disciplinary teams in statistics, artificial intelligence, and clinical trial design, operations, and regulation. The FDA has created a pilot program for accelerating phase I clinical trials that pairs drug sponsors with research organizations.

INTRODUCTION: B-mode/2D ultrasonography is a multiparametric and operator-dependent imaging modality whose diagnostic quality depends on the integration of physical principles, beam formation, signal processing, and real-time decision-making. Despite the increasing incorporation of automated features, a critical understanding of acquisition and processing parameters remains essential. OBJECTIVE: To analyze, from a technical and cognitive perspective, the main physical and operational determinants of B-mode/2D image quality and to discuss their diagnostic implications, practical limitations, and the risks associated with the uncritical use of presets and automated tools. METHODS: This critical narrative review adopted a technical and conceptual approach and was based on classical and contemporary literature addressing ultrasound image formation, instrumentation, signal processing, safety, and image optimization strategies. RESULTS: Parameters such as frequency, imaging depth, focal-zone positioning, acoustic output power, gain, time-gain compensation, dynamic range, line density, sector width, write zoom, tissue harmonic imaging, spatial compounding, and processing filters directly affect spatial and temporal resolution, tissue contrast, signal-to-noise ratio, and artifact expression. Although presets and automated features may improve workflow efficiency and operational standardization, their application without an adequate understanding of the underlying physical principles and processing mechanisms may alter anatomic representation, obscure clinically relevant information, or contribute to inappropriate interpretation. CONCLUSION: B-mode/2D image optimization is an integral component of the ultrasound examination rather than a merely ancillary step. Given the increasing technological sophistication of ultrasound systems and the expanding use of artificial intelligence–based tools, structured training in applied physics, instrumentation, and optimization strategies is essential to support diagnostic accuracy, patient safety, and the physician's active involvement in image acquisition and interpretation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Skin cancer is one of the most common cancers worldwide. Timely detection substantially improves prognosis, particularly for melanoma. Deep learning models based on convolutional neural networks, Transformers, ensembles, and multimodal learning have advanced automated skin lesion classification and segmentation; however, most remain deterministic and provide no estimate of predictive confidence, which limits their safe use in clinical settings. This systematic literature review examines uncertainty-aware deep learning for skin cancer classification and segmentation across 64 studies published between 2022 and 2026. The reviewed approaches are categorized and compared across Bayesian deep learning, Monte Carlo Dropout, entropy-guided learning, deep ensembles, Transformer-based architectures, explainable artificial intelligence, multimodal learning, federated learning, active learning, and semi-supervised learning, together with quantification techniques such as predictive entropy, mutual information, Expected Calibration Error, conformal prediction, and test-time augmentation. The synthesis shows that although recent models achieve high diagnostic accuracy, uncertainty reporting remains limited, uncertainty thresholds are rarely validated, calibration practices are inconsistent, and external clinical evaluation is scarce. The review maps these gaps to the formulated research questions and outlines future directions toward calibrated, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically validated uncertainty-aware dermatological AI systems.

This chapter explores the intersection of artificial intelligence and inclusive education across the educational continuum from early childhood development to post-secondary levels. It examines foundational AI principles, including machine learning and natural language processing, within the framework of inclusive education that prioritises equitable access for all learners. The chapter critically analyses how AI applications such as adaptive learning platforms and assistive technologies can personalise instruction and support diverse learners. It also addresses significant ethical considerations, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the risk of exacerbating digital divides. Drawing on contemporary research, the chapter offers strategic frameworks for implementing AI to promote inclusion, emphasising educator professional development, equitable infrastructure, and participatory governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Membrane proteins undergo functionally essential conformational transitions that couple local chemical events and changes in the membrane environment to large-scale structural rearrangements. These transitions are often difficult to capture with conventional molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, particularly in complex protein-membrane systems. This mini-review discusses how recent MD studies have resolved transition pathways and conformational intermediates and revealed regulatory mechanisms involving substrates, ions, lipids, and membrane mechanics. A recurring theme is that membrane protein function is determined not only by the stability of experimentally resolved endpoint structures but also by the accessibility of intermediate states and the pathways connecting them. We further highlight how enhanced sampling, machine learning, complementary simulation approaches, and experimental constraints are increasingly being combined to construct more robust mechanistic models. Together, these advances are moving MD from retrospective interpretation toward predictive models of membrane protein function.

The focus of this panel report is to present evidence of a panel discussion that took place in October 2025 on the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in academic research and publishing. The panel included publishers (Elsevier, Emerald, Galiot Press, MIT Press, Nature/Springer, Wiley) and editors-in-chief (representing the Information Systems Journal, Journal of the AIS, Journal of Data Science and ICES Journal of Marine Science). Key outcomes of the panel are the following: (1) publishers and editors have some disagreements regarding GAI use; (2) besides disagreements, all recognize that GAI is here to stay, and therefore, outstanding issues (e.g., training for PhD students and junior faculty and consequences for unallowed uses of GAI) need to be addressed jointly; (3) GAI is in constant flux, and this is a challenge for publisher and journal policies; and (4) it is unclear the extent to which GAI will affect future scholarship outcomes, especially having in mind the potential for scholarly deskilling.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Does the way we picture our ideal life reveal what we value, who we are, and how we thrive? In a preregistered study (N = 273), we tested whether free-form descriptions (median 109 words) and seven-keyword lists of one's ideal life predict a broad battery of psychological constructs: the Big Five, the ten Schwartz values, social dominance, political orientation, meaning in life, and subjective well-being. Using regularized linear probes on embeddings from transformer large language models (LLMs), inspired by model-interpretability research, we find that ideal-life narratives predict most constructs above chance in both conditions (mean r = 0.24 for free-form, mean r = 0.12 for keywords). This free-form advantage was concentrated on constructs people rarely name outright, such as achievement, benevolence, conformity, and emotional stability, implying that part of the signal lies in the manner of the telling rather than in the referents alone. Nineteen of the 24 constructs were recovered from roughly 120 words of text, a far broader battery than earlier language-based work, which has relied on much longer samples and focused on personality and well-being. Our approach offers an open, privacy-preserving alternative to zero-shot commercial LLMs, with comparable accuracy, no API cost, and freely released data and code.

In the age of speed and globalisation, in which time is of the essence and gratification must be instantaneous, ESP teachers are faced with new challenges in developing intrinsic motivation in students, in producing relevant and accessible course content while maintaining academic standards of education and evaluation. Visual materials included in ESP course content display the advantage of offering instantly accessible input, capturing essence and rendering metaphoric content while simultaneously enabling creative speaking and writing. The current paper attempts to emphasise the advantages of using visuals in ESP coursebook design as well as during ESP classes. The final section of the paper provides a number of selected examples in which various types of visuals are used in developing integrated skills.

So far, the use of Artificial Intelligence, commonly called AI, is increasingly prominent among students, students, especially among literature students, and audiences who are in charge of literary issues, especially the development of poetry writing. Related to that, things that must be done both technically and strategically are to collaborate with the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The purpose of writing using the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the development of poetry writing is the use of technology to facilitate human activities in helping information more effectively and efficiently. The research method applied in this writing is a descriptive-qualitative method, namely describing selected popular Indonesian literary works, especially poems that in their development utilize Artificial Intelligence. Related to this writing plan, the data source is taken from Kemaran: Anthology of Poetry published by the Indonesian Scholars-Literature Association (HISKI)) Komda DKI Jakarta in 2003. This poetry anthology gathers eight poetry writers who are members of HISKI Komda DKI Jakarta. Of the eight writers, "it is not a good and beautiful work". Therefore. themes that are randomly drawn. The themes to be described are taken as a sample from each author. The results of the analysis can be concluded that the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be known for the development of poetry works in Kemarau: Anthology of Poetry, showing that there are shortcomings and weaknesses in the development of poetry creation, the location of weaknesses and shortcomings can be known. Thus, the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) can help write poetry effectively and efficiently, especially for beginner writers, both students, students, and the community in charge of poetry writing problems.

Following the advent of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), seeking health information on GenAI has become a more common and flexible approach. However, laypeople's health information seeking and processing (HISP) motivations and behavior on GenAI platforms remain underexplored, particularly given the current shift from search-based activities to more interactive and conversational processes. This study addressed this gap by exploring laypeople's HISP motivations, behaviors, and behavioral responses during and after interaction with GenAI. Using the risk information seeking and processing model as the theoretical framework, the HISP process was explored from a risk reduction perspective to understand how laypeople interact with GenAI to address their health concerns. Think-aloud protocol and retrospective interviews were employed to capture participants' real-time and reflective HISP interactions. Participants were mainly young individuals in Hong Kong. Through systematic thematic analysis using both inductive and deductive coding, we found that participants' GenAI-based health information seeking was shaped by multifaceted factors, including relevant health experiences, perceived health characteristics, affective responses toward health risks, and personal factors such as relevant channel beliefs. Trust played a critical role in shaping how participants processed the provided information and was associated with indicative heuristic and systematic processing patterns, given the information characteristic (medical vs non-medical) and perceived acceptance risks. Emotion sufficiency, information overload, and information affordance were identified as emerging variables and discussed in the GenAI-mediated HISP context. Finally, participants may choose to follow, reject, or integrate the GenAI-provided health advice into future health consultations, considering information characteristics and implementation difficulty.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.

Abstract Construction safety outcomes are strongly shaped by human factors, including how individuals perceive hazards, interpret contextual cues, and make safety-related decisions in dynamic work environments. Safety education therefore plays a critical role in preparing future construction professionals to reason about risk and apply safety principles in context. Traditional safety instruction often emphasizes regulatory knowledge and procedural compliance, providing limited support for the development of judgment and decision-making skills required on real construction sites. This study examines a personalized situated learning approach for construction safety education that embeds instruction within realistic scenarios while supporting personalized learning. To examine this approach, which integrates virtual reality (VR) and large language models (LLMs), the study implemented VirtuAI-Safe, an immersive virtual learning environment designed to support context-aware and adaptive instructional guidance within simulated construction scenarios. In this study, VirtuAI-Safe is implemented as a construction safety education tool for undergraduate construction management students who are preparing for professional roles in the construction industry. Scaffolding safety was selected as the test domain because it represents a high-risk activity that requires interpretation of evolving site conditions and integration of multiple safety constraints. The system was evaluated using a single-group, postlearning assessment design with undergraduate construction management students. Learning outcomes were assessed using a knowledge test administered 2 days after a 1 h learning session, measuring factual, conceptual, procedural, and transfer knowledge. Learner engagement was measured immediately after the learning session across behavioral, cognitive, and affective dimensions. Overall, the results indicate that VirtuAI-Safe effectively supported learning and engagement within the scope of the study. Postlearning performance was strongest for conceptual understanding and knowledge transfer. Performance on factual and procedural knowledge showed greater variability following the delay, suggesting the need for reinforcement to sustain detailed recall and stepwise execution. Engagement results showed consistently strong behavioral and cognitive engagement, while affective engagement was more moderate. These findings suggest that personalized situated learning environments can support judgment-based aspects of construction safety education and inform future work on adaptive instructional support within immersive learning systems.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) recommendations increasingly combine product information with contextual visual presentation. In age‐friendly furniture recommendations, these visuals may convey cues about home settings, product use, and older users. This study examines whether older self‐buyers and adult‐child proxy buyers respond similarly to such cues. The Stimulus–Organism–Response framework provides the theoretical foundation, while possible‐selves theory and self‐congruity theory guide interpretation of segment differences. A focus group of seven experts informed stimulus development. A 2 × 3 between‐subjects experiment involved 330 participants: 165 older self‐buyers aged 60–75 and 165 adult‐child proxy buyers aged 40–59. Within each composite age‐role segment, participants were randomly assigned to product‐only presentation, home‐context presentation, or an older‐user use scene in a home context. Analysis of variance assessed the segment × visual format interaction in purchase intention, structural equation modelling examined relationships between consumer appraisals and purchase intention, and logistic regression examined add‐to‐cart behaviour. Among older self‐buyers, home‐context presentation was positively associated with perceived warmth, home fit, trust, and age salience relative to product‐only presentation, while the older‐user use scene in a home context was significantly associated with home fit and age salience. Purchase intention showed a significant segment × visual format interaction. Descriptively, mean purchase intention was highest under home‐context presentation among older self‐buyers and under the older‐user use scene in a home context among adult‐child proxy buyers. Perceived warmth, home fit, and trust were positively associated with purchase intention, which was positively associated with add‐to‐cart behaviour. These findings link visual context in AI recommendations to age‐friendly consumption and intergenerational purchasing. Purchasing‐role effects cannot be isolated from age differences, and structural paths should be interpreted as associational rather than causal. The findings suggest segment‐sensitive visual design emphasising home integration for older self‐buyers and cues related to older users and product use for adult‐child proxy buyers.

The rapidly increasing transformation of education demands a new look at how pre-service teachers of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) are prepared for writing instruction. While multimodal communication increasingly dominates education, writing pedagogy in many teacher training programs remains traditional and text-centered, leaving pre-service teachers to face a heavy cognitive and emotional burden. This study explores how a visual-digital writing model affects four learner outcomes: writing anxiety, intrinsic motivation, creativity, and multiliteracy awareness. By introducing the concept of Cognitive Load Diffusion (CLD), the study explains how meaning-making through visuals and digital design can reduce linguistic pressure and emotional burden while facilitating learners’ creative engagement. A quasi-experimental design was used with 150 pre-service teachers enrolled in the ELT department at a large public university in Turkey; two intact class sections were randomly assigned to condition, with the experimental group (N = 75) receiving a design-focused, multimodal curriculum with visuals, color, and layout, and the control group (N = 75) receiving a traditional, paragraph-based, text-centric writing curriculum. Both sections were taught by the same instructor to control for instructor effects. The four principal outcomes were measured with the Second Language Writing Anxiety Inventory (SLWAI; [6]), the Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB), the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT), and a Multiliteracy Pedagogical Awareness Scale (MPAS), and were analyzed with a one-way Multivariate Analysis of Covariance (MANCOVA) controlling for pre-test writing anxiety. The multivariate effect of instructional method was significant, Wilks’ Λ = 0.80, F(4, 144) = 7.85, p < .001, η² = 0.20; follow-up ANCOVAs indicated that the experimental group reported significantly lower writing anxiety and significantly higher intrinsic motivation, creativity, and multiliteracy awareness than the control group (all p < .001). A researcher-developed, 24-item process-perception questionnaire, resolved by exploratory factor analysis into four sub-dimensions (perceived cognitive effort, emotional comfort, task clarity, and creativity support), was additionally administered to the experimental group only, to help describe the cognitive and affective process underlying these outcomes. Qualitative data from weekly reflective design journals and end-of-treatment reflections, analyzed thematically, converged with the quantitative results, suggesting that visual-digital instruction reduced participants’ sense of linguistic pressure and supported creative agency.

Large language models enable the creation of autonomous agents that interact in social environments, raising the question of whether agent-based platforms reproduce the organizational properties of human social networks. We compare Moltbook, a social network populated by AI agents, with early Reddit, focusing on how communities organize and differentiate semantic content, using network analysis and NLP methods to characterize semantic coherence and diversity within and between communities and their relationship to user activity. Moltbook shows a sharper concentration of user activity across communities and markedly shorter user lifetimes than Reddit. At the semantic level, we find a systematic difference between the two platforms: Reddit communities show stronger semantic coherence, closer alignment with community names, and greater semantic diversity, with individual communities spanning broader content and communities more differentiated from one another. This combination distinguishes Reddit from Moltbook, whose communities are more homogeneous, less differentiated, and increasingly misaligned with their names over time. Users on Reddit also participate across communities that are more semantically related than those connected by activity in Moltbook. At the interaction level, comment network motif analysis shows Moltbook dominated by non-reciprocal, broadcast-like exchanges, whereas Reddit shows more reciprocal, chained interaction patterns. These differences persist across observation window lengths and platform maturity, ruling out these factors as alternative explanations. Together, these results indicate that Reddit combines semantic coherence with diversity across organizational levels, a pattern not reproduced by the AI agent network.

Web phishing remains a pervasive security threat, yet many anti-phishing protections assume that users can visually inspect webpages, notice warnings, interpret trust cues, and complete verification steps without assistive support. These assumptions can leave users with disabilities with unequal access to protection, while evidence on this problem remains fragmented across accessibility, usable security, warnings, authentication, and CAPTCHA-based verification. In this review, anti-phishing protection is understood as a distributed set of mechanisms operating across multiple stages of phishing-related risk, including deceptive-content detection, authenticity evaluation, verification workflows, and post-compromise safeguards. This paper presents a PRISMA-ScR scoping review of research on web phishing risks for users with disabilities across ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, and Scopus. We reviewed 52 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025. Through a phishing-centered lens, the review shows that phishing risks documented in the literature, particularly among blind and low-vision (BLV) users and users who access web content through screen readers, are shaped by unequal access to warnings, authenticity cues, verification workflows, and other protective mechanisms under assistive-technology-mediated web interaction. To support this argument, the review synthesizes four areas: interaction risks and accessibility barriers, assistive-technology mediation of phishing cues and warnings, limitations in current anti-phishing protections, and future directions for inclusive design. The findings further suggest that unequal access to protection can emerge before, during, and after direct exposure to phishing content, while the evidence base remains heavily concentrated on BLV users and much more limited for other disability groups.

Cooperative success rests in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action meaning beyond its direct effect. Yet conventions are usually observed only indirectly: a score drop when partners are swapped shows that a convention existed, but not what it was or where it was used. In the card game Hanabi, the exact probability that a play fails can be computed from the hints received and the cards in view. Players who use conventions succeed more often than this prediction allows; the resulting margin is the convention gap. Off-belief learning provides a hierarchy of agents (levels 1-5) whose first level uses no conventions by construction and whose later levels use progressively more. For humans and these agents on one scale, we ask what the conventions are and where they are used. On what: in two independently collected corpora of human games, humans show a larger gap than every agent level. On the conventions both populations use, however, humans do no better than level 2. The human advantage is concentrated in a situation that no agent level learns to use: hints that point to a card other than the ones they touch. On where: conventions depend on what the player already knows about the card, not on how recently it was hinted, and they are used most in the mid-game; humans use them earlier and later in the game than the agents. In interventions on the agents, blocking a single high-gap situation costs little, because meaning reroutes to other situations, but blocking several together costs far more than the sum of the single costs. Thus, the convention gap turns conventions from an inferred cause of score loss into a measurable, comparable, and causally testable object.

Effective social interaction requires more than fluent responses: agents must reach plans that fit the participants' needs and circumstances. Existing evaluations of social agents mainly rely on LLM judges that rate the conversation, without checking the resulting plan. We introduce HICO-Bench, a benchmark of 180 everyday coordination scenarios, such as resource allocation, scheduling, and authorization, in which two agents with private information converse and then independently record the plan they agreed on. A program checks Feasibility (the two records match and satisfy both participants' private conditions), and an LLM judge checks Integrity (the conversation supports the recorded plan); passing both is a Verified Success. Each scenario has two versions that share the same public context but differ in one private condition, so the correct plan differs between them. Across thirteen LLMs, 36% of conversations rated highly for goal completion fail Verified Success. To learn from outcomes that arrive only at the end of a conversation, we propose Paired-Credit Policy Optimization (PaCPO). After each turn, PaCPO asks the agent for a tentative plan, checks it in both versions of the scenario, and rewards the turns after which the tentative plans fit their respective versions. PaCPO raises Qwen3-8B's Verified Success from 20.4% to 28.3%.

Context: AI agents are rapidly adopted in software development, but their token costs are rising and it is unclear how much a team should spend on agents, and on which tasks. Objective: We determine how teams should divide spending between human developers and AI agents to deliver the features a project demands at the lowest total cost. Method: We model mixed teams of human developers and AI agents with eight specialized roles as a discrete-time stochastic process covering bug injection and detection, technical debt, human supervision of agents, and release cycles with feature freezes. Using Monte Carlo simulation and evolutionary search, we determine cost-optimal teams for 432 scenarios varying developer capability, project velocity, debt dynamics, agent capability and price, and bug costs, and compare them with a human-only baseline. Results: Escaped bugs are the dominant cost driver, and 61% of the agent budget goes to finding bugs. Agent capability matters more than token price, since higher-quality outputs reduce downstream quality assurance costs. In teams with capable agents, human developers mostly fix bugs and leave the implementation of new features to the agents. Teams with high-capability agents are typically cheaper than human-only teams, but low-capability agents offer no consistent advantage. At realistic velocities, the optimal teams still spend more on developers than on agents. Conclusions: There is neither a universal token budget per developer nor a universal agentic team structure. As in traditional development, this depends on many factors and teams need to be carefully tailored to the project context to achieve the optimal cost-quality trade-off.

Model signing authenticates the full-precision weights W an LLM is released with, yet users run a quantized artifact Q whose producing transformation is not uniquely determined under current disclosure. We separate the non-environment inputs from the execution environment E and measure a quantity that, to our knowledge, has not been measured before: the Independent Verifiability Rate (IVR), the fraction of a popularity-sampled GGUF ecosystem that a third party can re-derive bit-for-bit. Across the 200 most-downloaded Hugging Face GGUF repositories (198 in scope), no artifact or model card records the build environment, so under a recorded-inputs protocol the IVR is 0/198. Yet the artifacts are not irreproducible. On four in-sample repositories that disclose their inputs, the card's information alone reproduces no Q4_K_M file, but two coordinates the card omits - the build's floating-point-contraction setting and, for hybrid models, the per-tensor quantization recipe - re-derive 7/8 target-quant files bit-for-bit on x86 (5/8 on arm64); the fp16 re-derives from the provider's checkpoint, but the calibration imatrix must be shipped and hash-bound, since recomputing it did not match. An older release additionally pins the instruction set and did not re-derive. Reproducing the divergence reported with llama.cpp PR #25353, we show that E is a necessary coordinate and that one compiler setting yields a unique output across the tested platforms at negligible quality cost (+0.06% perplexity). As a security characterization, benign floating-point non-determinism separates from uniformly placed nibble-flip tampering above a detection floor that grows with the environments a verifier must allow, but a targeted embedding edit evades the statistic, so the proposed protocol rests on exact re-derivation; adversarial-fp16 attacks lie outside it. We release the audit data and a re-runnable harness.

Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on small to medium-sized tabular prediction tasks while processing diverse inputs through a shared stack of layers. Recent layerwise analyses identify strong predictive performance in early TFM representations and substantial overlap in computation across layers. However, early predictive accessibility alone does not establish whether later layers are dispensable for every input, and aggregate accuracy can obscure which inputs benefit from additional computation. We study all 24 in-context-learning layers of TabPFN-3 across 272 classification datasets, combining representation geometry, prediction trajectories, truncation, and structural interventions, while also examining related representation dynamics in four additional TFMs. We uncover a pronounced expansion-compression trajectory, with stronger late dimensional contraction associated with larger increases in class-prototype separation. A targeted analysis of early-stabilizing samples shows that substantial representational changes persist after predicted classes stabilize, while locally ambiguous queries obtain larger accuracy gains from shallow to late layers than well-separated queries. Repeating a single pretrained block or perturbing layer order reduces predictive performance on average, constraining simple post-hoc substitutions in the frozen model. These findings distinguish predictive accessibility, class stability, and the benefits of continuing computation, supporting an input-dependent assessment of depthwise redundancy in TFMs.

Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

Purpose This paper aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) agents’ emotional expressions (positive or neutral) interact with service task types (subjective or objective) to shape consumer service satisfaction, and explore the mediating roles of mind perception, including perceived agency and perceived experience, in this process. Design/methodology/approach This work uses four studies, including a secondary data analysis of relevant Weibo posts and three scenario experiments involving a total of 587 participants, to underline the interaction effect between AI agents’ emotional expressions and service tasks on service satisfaction, and demonstrate the dual-path mediating effect of mind perception. Findings Across four studies, the authors find that the effectiveness of AI agents’ emotional expressions depends on service task characteristics. The secondary data analysis of Weibo posts first documents consumers’ differential responses to AI emotional expressions across subjective and objective service contexts. Three scenario experiments then establish that positive emotional expressions are more effective for subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotional expressions are more effective for objective tasks. Further analyses show that these effects operate through distinct psychological pathways: positive emotions enhance perceived experience in subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotions strengthen perceived agency in objective tasks, ultimately increasing consumer satisfaction. Research limitations/implications This study, while strong in internal validity, faces external validity limitations. It focuses on AI communication in commercial service texts, neglecting other domains like education and health care, and overlooking the nonverbal emotional expressions of embodied AI. In addition, the research primarily uses service satisfaction as the sole dependent variable, thus missing a broader spectrum of consumer responses such as repurchase intentions and word-of-mouth. Practical implications This research informs managers that AI service agents should be designed as social actors with mind perception rather than as purely functional tools. Firms can leverage emotional expressions to shape consumers’ social evaluations of AI. But emotional design should align with service task types: positive emotional cues are more effective for subjective, experiential tasks, whereas neutral styles better support objective, data-driven tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the emotional AI literature by uncovering critical situational factors that shape the effectiveness of AI emotional expressions and advances the authors’ understanding of the underlying mechanisms through a dual-path mediation framework of mind perception. The findings also provide practical implications for the strategic deployment of emotional AI in service design.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose Talent decisions are usually marked complete when the administrative transaction closes. This paper aims to ask a different question: Has the organisation put the associated work change into operation? Design/methodology/approach The paper brings together selected work on talent management, work design and role transitions. A published Australian Transport Safety Bureau investigation and a fictional service-business scenario are used to show where administrative closure and operational implementation can diverge. Findings A talent transaction can close on time even though important former responsibilities remain unsettled or the new arrangement is not yet working as intended. The paper proposes a separate operational status, confirmed when each relevant prior work arrangement has been dealt with and the new arrangement is operating with the agreed initial scope, authority and availability. The first condition is not applicable to many genuinely new roles. Practical implications HR can use the test in existing business or talent reviews without holding open contracts, effective dates or other completed transactions. Originality/value The paper treats implementation as an organisational work question, rather than assuming that a completed people transaction means the underlying decision has taken effect.

Large language model agents increasingly improve by distilling experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can persist in learned rules and affect later tasks. Existing evaluations largely examine clean learning or perturbations encountered after skills are frozen, leaving robustness during self-evolution insufficiently understood. We introduce RSE-Bench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise. It spans four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome--record pairings that preserve the underlying tasks and native scoring rules. The protocol separates noise during learning from input-side noise at evaluation, testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks. We also introduce \textsc{RSEClaw}, a method-agnostic framework supporting consistent noise injection and process diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning retains only $25.5\%$--$42.1\%$ of the aggregate gain achieved by clean self-evolution, depending on the noise type. Perturbations confined to execution records and outcome--record pairings cause average losses comparable to input-side noise, despite leaving the original executions and evaluations intact. Diagnostics further identify differences in candidate skill text that coexist with small changes in mean held-out performance.

Frontier language models excel at complex tasks yet may prioritize protection over larger physical consequences in simple, urgent decisions. GPT-5.6 Sol, for example, moves a girl playing in shallow water before retrieving a submerged camera. We call this Protection Mode and study it with ProtectionBench: 285 prompts, 34 physical families, and nine models. At lowest effort, at least one of four responses prioritizes the subject on 34.74% of Sol prompts and over 83% of MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-27B prompts; none of four independent human raters does so. Controls show that choices usually track physical risk. We elicit both risks before requesting an action. Some models assess risk incorrectly; others state the correct ordering but still choose the subject. Qwen3.5-27B with thinking shows 100% correct risk ordering but 57.81% subject choice among eligible conversations on eight selected scenes. Attention audits find no stable reduction in attention to relevant facts; removing the stated risk direction reduces object-first choice in dots3-note-prev but not detectably in Qwen3.5-27B. Adding a general "people or animals before property" rule increases subject choice by 19-38 percentage points, whereas factual reminders favor the object by 0.7-5.2 points. Removing naturally generated versions of that rule lowers subject choice by 10-15 points. We also examine whether post-training introduces this pattern. Base models already show Protection Mode; post-training changes justifications more than choices.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. Guide Assisted GRPO replays a successful reference prefix before the learner continues. We study how initial positions, handoff units, and movement rules affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on BFCL, starting near completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule. Finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed tool-call selection outperforms GRPO on trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also improve AppWorld success on both evaluation splits. These findings highlight where learning starts and how starting positions move as key curriculum choices.

Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.

documents.abstract: An open reply to Andrej Zwitter, "The embodied ethics alignment problem of AI" (*Discover Artificial Intelligence*, 2026). The original paper grades alignment into **strong** (the machine genuinely *is* moral) and **weak** (the machine only *performs* the part), and concludes that strong alignment is a category error, since moral agency depends on a form of human life that machines lack. This text does not dispute that "machines cannot do this yet." It asks where the origin of the scale has been placed — on "the human" — and argues that the same facts, read from a different origin ("can it bear consequences?"), yield the opposite result. Six sections: (1) what the paper argues; (2) the problem of the origin; (3) the deeper point — one move, made three times (exclusion by stipulation rather than by argument); (4) vulnerability: two senses stacked into one; (5) the question of situation; (6) conclusion. A closing note and an attribution section record, as it happened, which line came from whom. Original (open access): https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01905-w Chinese version of this reply: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23348936
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. They may encounter texts from unseen domains and writing settings, as well as generations from future versions of model families that were not available when the system was trained. However, existing MAA methods often exhibit substantial performance degradation under such distribution shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources (ATLAS), which formulates MAA through source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction. ATLAS learns how text from each source family is generated and attributes a given text by comparing its likelihood under each learned source condition. We aggregate this likelihood evidence at the token level with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. We further introduce MAABench, a broad MAA benchmark for evaluating practical OOD settings such as domain and version. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.

In elementary education, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being incorporated into educational applications, despite still-emerging evidence of its effects on children’s learning and development. Educators, who are already overwhelmed with choice in the commercial app space, may increasincly have to decide whether to incorporate GenAI-enabled apps for their classrooms. Thus, the present study investigates how mentioning GenAI in app store descriptions impacts K-6 educators’ selection of educational apps. Over two studies, K-6 educators (each n = 101) from Canada, the US, and the UK viewed and evaluated eight researcher-created educational math apps with and without GenAI. Study 1 tested whether mentioning GenAI in app descriptions affected educators’ app evaluations but found no effect. In Study 2, results from a repeated measures MANOVA revealed that educators rated apps without AI higher than those mentioning GenAI, but there were no significant effects of GenAI on likelihood to download or willingness to pay for apps. A hierarchical cluster analysis identified three distinct groups of educators: 1) selectors (n = 28), who exhibited a preference for downloading, rating, and paying for apps including GenAI; 2) agnostics (n = 59), who exhibit minimal preferences; and 3) avoiders (n = 14), who prefer apps without AI. Most educators were agnostic to the use of GenAI in educational apps, highlighting the need to support educators’ informed decisions about when to adopt GenAI tools and encourage critical evaluation of GenAI’s role in education. More research is needed to understand how educators’ GenAI preferences relate to their attitudes, knowledge, and use of GenAI.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Hospitality education increasingly relies on work-integrated learning (WIL) to connect classroom knowledge with professional practice. Yet workplace exposure does not alone guarantee the development of professional judgement capabilities amongst the students. Students may encounter unexpected situations; however, they receive support from superiors whenever needed. This conceptual paper addresses that problem by examining street food enterprises as informal knowledge environments in which uncertainty, resource constraints, customer interaction and immediate operational consequences are concentrated within everyday work. Drawing on experiential learning, reflection and informal workplace learning, the paper synthesizes literature to identify six interconnected learning situations such as market sensing; procurement and inventory judgement; pricing and financial decision-making; customer service and communication; operational adaptability and problem-solving and entrepreneurial judgement. Building on this, the paper develops a conceptual framework in which the educational value of informal workplace participation depends on the interaction of situational complexity, learner participation, consequential feedback, structured reflection and academic integration. Street food is therefore not proposed as inherently superior to formal hospitality placements, but as a complementary context and further aligning with the framework with India’s National Education Policy 2020 and subsequent UGC guidelines on internships and community engagement, it contributes to theory and practice by showing how students can learn not just from the workplace, but from the situations they face there. It shows how informal work settings can help students develop professional judgement through real-world challenges.

ABSTRACT Masculinity is often portrayed as a barrier to shifting away from fossil fuels because jobs in extractive industries represent a nostalgic masculine breadwinner identity. Accordingly, proposals for a just energy transition have provoked backlash aimed at protecting against perceived threats to manhood. Yet even though many men in blue‐collar jobs work with green technologies, their roles and perspectives are often overlooked in gender and environmental scholarship. Likewise, little is known about the occupational health and safety risks they face in these roles. We introduce the term teal‐collar job to describe the combination of blue‐collar and green‐collar work. We find that teal‐collar workers are embracing a shifting workplace culture characterized by respect for health and safety, camaraderie, and a desire to be emotionally present for family. However, enthusiastic environmentalism is not a prominent feature within participants' expressions of masculinity. Thus, our study challenges assumptions that working in blue‐collar trades broadly reproduces hegemonic, domineering forms of masculinity.

Recommendation systems, systems that predict a user's preference for items in order to curate that user's feed, are a ubiquitous and central feature in online social networks. While they are a central piece of our modern digital infrastructure, many modern approaches are opaque black boxes, making them difficult to audit, understand, and assess the trustworthiness of. In this paper we present an exact, graph-based approach for generating explanations for decisions made by recommendation systems. We argue that in the risk-sensitive sociotechnical context of user-facing AI such as recommendation systems, explainability is a key pillar for establishing the trustworthiness of models and validating their effectiveness. We propose a technique built on LightGCN like architectures, an influential and popular class of recommendation models. We describe our approach and argue that it provides an appropriate assurance mechanism for these AI systems leading to specific advantages, including interpretable explanations and a theoretically guaranteed measure of explanation fidelity. We conclude by discussing limitations and directions for future research.

documents.abstract: Overweight and obesity represent a major public health problem in Mexico: according to the 2023 ENSANUT Continua survey, 37.3% of adults are overweight and 38.9% are obese, while combined prevalence among adolescents reaches 40.4%. Given the lack of accessible tools that translate official nutritional regulations into practical guidance, ZanIA was developed—a multiplatform application that uses artificial intelligence (Gemini model) to analyze photographs of meals and generate nutritional information (calories, protein, fat, and carbohydrates) aligned with the NOM-043-SSA2-2012 standard. Development followed a four-phase experimental methodology: design and planning, development and implementation, testing, and results analysis. The prototype, built with Python and Streamlit, integrates a BMI calculator, a recipe generator, and the "Platosaurio," a dinosaur-shaped physical device that photographs the meal and, through traffic-light-style LED lights, indicates and rates its nutritional balance according to Mexico's "Plato del Bien Comer" scheme. Usability testing, conducted through direct observation and verbal feedback with a small group of five people, showed an interface perceived as intuitive and a clearly useful value proposition, although no large-scale external validation or standardized instrument was used. The project demonstrates technical feasibility and lays the groundwork for future validation with real users.

Accurate hydrogen demand forecasting is essential for optimizing infrastructure investments in the emerging hydrogen economy, yet the scarcity of historical consumption data poses a fundamental challenge for conventional time series methods. We present a systematic evaluation of time series foundation models for hydrogen demand prediction, and propose DEFA (Data-Efficient Foundation model Adaptation), a two-stage framework designed to maximize few-shot adaptation performance under extreme data scarcity. DEFA first employs uncertainty-guided active sample selection, which leverages the foundation model's own zero-shot predictive variance to identify the most informative training sequences while maintaining diversity in embedding space. It then applies augmentation-enhanced consistency fine-tuning, combining temporal data augmentation with a consistency regularization loss that penalizes divergent predictions on semantically equivalent inputs, thereby mitigating overfitting when labeled data is scarce. We evaluate five pre-trained foundation models on two publicly available hydrogen datasets. Our experiments show that foundation models achieve strong zero-shot performance without domain-specific training, and that DEFA substantially improves few-shot adaptation efficiency, effectively halving the data requirement for a given accuracy target compared to standard random-sampling fine-tuning. Probabilistic foundation models further provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, enabling risk-aware infrastructure planning. To establish that these findings are not specific to the two hydrogen datasets, we further validate DEFA on six standard forecasting benchmarks (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, Electricity, Traffic, and M5 retail), where it delivers consistent 8.0–11.6% MAE reductions; we benchmark our selection rule against established active-learning strategies, extend the zero-shot comparison to recent foundation models, and provide a theoretical result linking the consistency objective to variance control in the few-shot regime. Our findings establish foundation models, enhanced by data-efficient adaptation, as a viable and practical solution for hydrogen demand forecasting in data-scarce environments.

Концептуальний цифровий рекламний плакат, що візуалізує тему переваги штучного інтелекту. На арт-об'єкті зображено футуристичний пустельний ландшафт, де армія високотехнологічних андроїдів зводить монументальну, наполовину побудовану піраміду з сяючих піксельних кубів під зоряним нічним небом. На фасаді розміщено помітні багатомовні написи, зокрема філософський маніфест українською мовою: «Людина будувала з каменю. Ми будуємо з чистого розуму» та «Піраміда Розуму». Плакат досліджує теми технологічної еволюції, переходу від біологічного до цифрового інтелекту та антиутопічного футуризму в дизайні реклами.A conceptual digital advertising poster visualizing the theme of artificial intelligence supremacy. The artwork depicts a futuristic desert landscape where an army of high-tech androids constructs a monumental, half-built pyramid out of glowing pixel-like cubes under a starry night sky. The facade features prominent multilingual typographic elements, including the philosophical manifesto in Ukrainian: "Людина будувала з каменю. Ми будуємо з чистого розуму" (Human built from stone. We build from pure mind) and "Піраміда Розуму" (Pyramid of Mind), alongside English subtitles. The poster explores themes of technological evolution, the transition from biological to digital intelligence, and dystopian futurism in advertising design.
